source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

terms.definition: A neural network trained on large amounts of text that can generate and interpret language. Here LLMs act as agents that call spreadsheet tools to read and edit workbooks.
One of the most capable, recently released AI models from the leading labs, such as the GPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok models tested here.
A section of a financial model that tracks each loan's balance, interest, repayments and borrowings period by period.
A company's formal correction of financial statements it previously published, usually because they contained errors.
A plain-text file format for a single flat table, with no formulas, formatting or multiple sheets.
Slide presentations that bankers prepare to pitch a deal or service to clients.
A valuation method that projects a company's future cash flows and discounts them back to today's value using a required rate of return.
The blended rate of return a company must pay its lenders and shareholders, commonly used as the discount rate in a DCF.
A table in a deal model listing where the money for a transaction comes from (debt, equity, cash) and what it is spent on; the two sides must total the same.
Firms that buy and manage companies with investor money, often funded partly by debt, and whose analysts build detailed financial models of those deals.
A unit equal to one hundredth of a percentage point, so 1,000 bp is 10 percentage points.
The percentage of the value of pledged collateral (such as inventory) that a lender is willing to lend against.
A span of time at the start of a financing arrangement before repayments are due.
Kept private and used only for testing, so that models cannot have seen the tasks during training.
A deliberate change to an input value made to test how a model's dependent outputs respond. In this paper it is also the name of a rubric category.
A benchmark US interest rate to which many floating-rate loans are pegged, with a spread added on top.
Shorthand for two finance careers whose junior analysts spend much of their time building and modifying spreadsheet models.
The starting spreadsheet given to a task author, which they modify or build on to create a benchmark task.
Legally protected creative or proprietary work; here, concerns that a submitted spreadsheet might belong to someone else.
Typed in as a fixed number rather than calculated by a formula that refers to other cells.
The allowed margin of difference between a computed value and the reference value, such as ±2%, within which the value still counts as correct.
A spreadsheet error value shown when a formula refers to a cell that no longer exists or is invalid.
The software around a model during evaluation: the tools it can call, the prompt it gets and the loop that runs it.
A free, open-source office suite whose spreadsheet engine can recalculate formulas; 'headless' means it runs without a visible interface.
A spreadsheet setting that lets circular references (formulas that depend on their own results) be computed by repeating the calculation until the values settle.
A Python library for reading and writing Excel workbook files.
A restricted environment in which code can run without access to files, the network or the wider system.
Standing instructions given to a language model before the task itself, setting its role and rules.
Extra structure around a model, such as planning steps, specialised prompts or helper tools, designed to improve its performance.
A statistic measuring how much several raters agree beyond what chance would produce; 1 means perfect agreement and 0 means chance-level.
A classification accuracy score that balances precision and recall, computed separately for each class and then averaged so each class counts equally.
A provider setting that controls how much internal step-by-step thinking a model does before answering, trading cost and time for quality.
A benchmark of long-horizon software engineering tasks in which agents must fix real code repositories.
A separate benchmark of question-answering tasks over financial spreadsheets built from U.S. Treasury Bulletin data.
A task format in which a system must answer questions, here about the contents of a spreadsheet.
Relating to a balance sheet, the financial statement listing a company's assets, liabilities and equity, where assets must equal liabilities plus equity.
The units of text a language model generates; providers charge per token, so more output means higher cost.

terms.expansion: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization
terms.definition: A common measure of a company's operating profit before financing costs, taxes and non-cash charges.
A revolving credit facility: a loan a company can draw on, repay and draw again up to a limit, often used to cover cash shortfalls.
Spending on long-lived physical assets such as equipment or buildings.
The day-to-day costs of running a business, such as rent, salaries and utilities.
A headline metric used to track a business's performance; a KPI Dashboard collects such metrics in one place.
The financial statement showing a company's revenue, expenses and profit over a period.
Marks or ranges showing the uncertainty around a reported number, for example from repeated runs or confidence intervals.
An average computed by pooling all tasks together so each task counts equally, as opposed to a macro average that first averages within groups and then averages the groups.
